title: Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a model that predicts what will happen when a robot touches, pushes, grasps, inserts, or deforms an object accurately enough to plan useful actions on previously unseen real tasks. Its predictions would include contact forces and object motion, with quantified errors over a declared operating domain. The target is transfer without per-task system identification or real-robot fine-tuning.

Concept definition: the model could use explicit mechanics, learned action-conditioned predictions, or a hybrid. A planner would use it to compare possible actions and their physical consequences. A learned world model qualifies only if its force and motion predictions are tested and calibrated on held-out real interactions. A policy that performs a trained skill, or a video predictor that produces plausible-looking motion, does not by itself establish this capability. The world-model literature provides a basis for planning through predicted rollouts while identifying physical validity as a separate challenge from visual realism.

significance.text: Conditional impact assessment: predictive mechanics allows engineers to evaluate designs before fabrication. Comparable reliability for robotic contact could let a planner evaluate manipulation strategies before trying them on hardware, replacing substantial task-specific experimentation and data collection with engineering calculation within a validated domain. This would be a major enabling advance because inaccurate or difficult-to-obtain models remain an obstacle in contact-rich control. The analogy expresses the proposed benefit; it does not imply that existing engineering mechanics predicts every contact interaction reliably.

Assembly and insertion are plausible beneficiaries where the model covers the relevant geometry, friction, forces, and clearances. Extending that benefit to cloth, cables, and soft objects would require corresponding validation, adequate sensing, and tractable planning. Accurate contact prediction alone would not resolve uncertain object state, limited robot controllability, or the search for a feasible action sequence. The contact-rich-task survey specifically identifies sensing and modeling difficulties in deformable-object manipulation.

The advance would build on a diverse existing field that includes model-based control, simulation-trained policies, learning from real data, and hybrid approaches. Some simulation-trained policies already transfer to hardware without task-specific real-world policy learning, while still using hardware calibration and actuator identification. ROB-07 therefore targets a stronger predictive planning capability rather than assuming that every useful manipulation policy must be repaired with real task data.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is reliable prediction across changing contact conditions, coupled to a planner that succeeds on new hardware tasks. Contact dynamics are hybrid: the governing equations and active constraints can change abruptly as an interaction moves between free motion, impact, sticking, and sliding. Small changes in geometry, material properties, or contact configuration can alter the outcome. These are documented barriers, but the supplied evidence does not establish the field-wide absence of every model that might satisfy the proposed target.

Simulation discrepancies are particularly consequential for frictional sticking and sliding, small-clearance contacts, and deformation. A model can reproduce broad motion while mispredicting whether an insertion jams, a grasp slips, or a soft object changes shape in a useful way. Improving prediction therefore requires handling contact-mode transitions and geometry and material variation, rather than treating hybrid contact as the sole remaining obstacle.

Proposed engineering requirement: prediction errors must be characterized at the horizons and under the interactions a planner actually uses. The system must distinguish conditions where its predictions are dependable from conditions outside its demonstrated coverage, and prediction and planning must be fast enough for the intended manipulation. Whether this is best achieved through compact theory, a calibrated learned model, or a hybrid remains unresolved.

current_state.text: Zhang and colleagues’ Safe Learning for Contact-Rich Robot Tasks, arXiv version 4 revised October 29, 2026, describes uncertainty, complex and discontinuous dynamics, and damage risk in contact-rich interaction. Its discussion covers abrupt contact-mode changes, geometry and material variation, and simulation discrepancies involving friction, small clearances, and deformation. These findings document substantial obstacles and existing approaches; they do not establish that all approaches fail the ROB-07 target. The supplied review had the landing-page abstract and a PDF extraction ending during page 37, with the relevant passages retained. The landing-page and PDF abstracts differ in wording but agree substantively.

Pan, Coros, Malik, and Lin’s May 27, 2026 arXiv paper reports zero-shot simulation-to-real policy transfer on a multi-fingered hand for two blind tasks: peg-in-hole insertion and ball balancing. The policies use proprioception and contact observations, including a designed center-of-pressure representation. This is a concrete demonstration of a useful tactile representation and task-policy transfer, rather than a demonstration of a general contact model used by a planner on held-out tasks.

The scope of that transfer matters. Pan and colleagues’ implementation uses only the surface-normal component of the contact representation because simulated shear estimates were unreliable. It also includes sensor calibration using paired rollouts and actuator system identification. These procedures coexist with the reported zero-shot policy transfer; zero-shot does not mean that no hardware alignment occurred. The supplied review had a complete text extraction through the paper’s references and appendices. The result does not by itself establish calibrated force-and-motion prediction, deformable-task coverage, or the proposed planning capability.

Li and colleagues’ A Comprehensive Survey on World Models for Embodied AI, arXiv version 3 revised June 25, 2026, describes policies or planners reasoning over predicted rollouts and identifies physical-consistency evaluation as an open challenge. Appearance-level realism can coexist with physically implausible or causally inconsistent predictions. The supplied review retained the relevant discussion on page 16, although the PDF extraction truncated during references on page 20. This supports distinguishing convincing video prediction from the tested contact-force and motion prediction required here.

The earlier research also attributed an open-problem statement about dexterous manipulation to Billard and Kragic’s 2019 Trends and challenges in robot manipulation. No retained artifact was available in the supplied review, so neither that attribution nor the earlier account of abstract-only access can be verified here. This limitation does not invalidate the other documented results.

Evidence scope: the supplied material documents results and discussions dated May, June, and October 2026. Retrieval on November 1, 2026 does not establish comprehensive coverage through that date because the supplied freshness search record is empty. Pan’s result and Li’s survey are presented here as arXiv reports. The research notes describe Zhang’s survey as accepted by npj Robotics, but the supplied review does not independently establish that publication status. Taken together, these sources motivate the innovation without establishing either its achievement or its categorical absence across the field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: pre-register a hardware task suite containing rigid frictional interactions and deformable-object tasks, with none of the evaluation tasks used to fit the predictive model. Freeze the model before evaluation. A planner should use that model, task goals, and explicitly declared sensor observations, without a task-specific demonstration policy, per-task identification, or real-robot fine-tuning. Disclose any reusable robot or sensor calibration and actuator identification so that the transfer claim has a clear meaning.
completion_criteria.label: Frozen model plans held-out rigid and deformable tasks without fine-tuning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed prediction assessment: publish force and motion errors on held-out hardware interactions, specifying prediction horizons, uncertainty coverage levels, and the operating domain. Evaluate whether the claimed bounds remain calibrated across the contact modes, materials, geometries, and deformation regimes included in that domain. Report failures and conditions outside coverage. These are proposed requirements for a convincing demonstration, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Held-out force-and-motion error bounds calibrated across the operating domain

completion_criteria.text: Proposed task assessment: compare the planner’s hardware success with a policy trained on real demonstrations of the same evaluation tasks. Pre-register trial counts, comparability margins, and safety constraints, and disclose each system’s data and calibration allowances. Release sufficient model, planner, task, calibration, and measurement detail for independent replication. Replication on another setup would strengthen the evidence that the result extends beyond a particular laboratory implementation.
completion_criteria.label: Planner hardware success versus same-task real-demonstration policy

completion_criteria.text: Interpretation of completion: a successful finite suite would establish demonstrated breadth within its tested domain, not literal universality across manipulation. Claims about cloth, cables, other soft objects, or new robot embodiments would require corresponding evidence. Pan and colleagues’ two zero-shot policy transfers are an enabling result, but do not alone meet this proposed demonstration because they do not establish the frozen predictive planner, force-and-motion error bounds, and rigid-plus-deformable coverage specified here.
completion_criteria.label: Finite-suite success shows breadth only within the tested domain

related_concepts.text: Editorial comparison with ROB-01, Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments: ROB-01 concerns carrying out instructions in unfamiliar settings, while ROB-07 supplies a narrower capability for predicting the physical consequences of contact actions. The historical idea of an embodied common-sense physical reasoning engine overlaps ROB-07 where it makes tested physical predictions; ordinary-language task interpretation and choice belong with ROB-01. The historical description and full ROB-01 record were not supplied, so this is a proposed conceptual boundary based on the available material.

Editorial comparison with ROB-02, Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability: better contact prediction could support dexterity, but prediction and planning are distinct from demonstrating a complete dexterous system at human reliability. Likewise, ROB-09, Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills, concerns continued skill acquisition and retention. ROB-07 instead proposes testing a frozen predictive model on new tasks; ongoing learning could complement that capability without being the same breakthrough.

Editorial comparison with ROB-03, An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot, and ROB-05, Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines: these entries concern actuation and physical embodiment. Their systems might benefit from predictive contact or deformation models, but successful modeling would not establish useful artificial muscles or reconfigurable load-bearing matter, and those embodiments would not by themselves establish ROB-07.

Editorial comparison with ROB-04, Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock, and ROB-08, Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material: predictive manipulation could be an enabling component in fabrication, assembly, and material handling. Their defining outcomes remain self-reproduction and collective construction, respectively, which require capabilities beyond contact prediction.

Editorial comparison with ROB-06, Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body, and ROB-10, Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients: contact prediction may overlap with physical interaction in these settings, but ROB-07’s general hardware demonstrations would not establish either medical outcome. Conversely, a successful medical intervention or procedure would not automatically demonstrate transferable contact prediction across unrelated manipulation tasks. These distinctions use the supplied roster titles; full records for the other entries were not available.

change_log.change: Reframed the categorical claim that the contact model is missing as a target capability whose field-wide absence is not established.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence documents substantial barriers, but the supplied search coverage cannot support an exhaustive absence claim.

change_log.change: Expanded the barrier explanation to include discontinuous contact transitions, geometry and material variation, friction, small clearances, deformation, and sensing.
change_log.reason: The review supplies useful technical distinctions and shows that hybrid contact is not the sole obstacle.

change_log.change: Replaced the exhaustive simulation-versus-demonstration account with model-based, learned, simulation-trained, and hybrid approaches.
change_log.reason: The reviewed literature includes classical and hybrid controllers, and Pan reports transfer without task-specific real-world policy learning.

change_log.change: Qualified broad task-family benefits and retained the engineering analogy as a conditional impact assessment.
change_log.reason: Contact prediction could reduce experimentation within a validated domain, but does not automatically provide perception, controllability, planning, or competence across all deformable objects.

change_log.change: Preserved Pan’s two-task zero-shot result while adding its policy-transfer scope, normal-force restriction, sensor calibration, and actuator identification.
change_log.reason: These details explain what was demonstrated without treating calibration as a contradiction of zero-shot policy transfer.

change_log.change: Updated source-access descriptions using the supplied review and retained the Billard–Kragic attribution only with an explicit verification limitation.
change_log.reason: The review includes relevant PDF passages for Zhang and Li, complete extracted text for Pan, and no retained artifact for Billard and Kragic.

change_log.change: Made the completion proposal assessable through frozen-model evaluation, declared observations and calibration, error horizons and coverage, comparison margins, safety constraints, and reproducibility.
change_log.reason: These details resolve ambiguity in 'only the model' and distinguish proposed demonstration criteria from achieved results or established standards.

change_log.change: Added explicit limits on finite-suite generalization and on freshness through November 1, 2026.
change_log.reason: Finite tests establish tested breadth, and retrieval dates do not substitute for a comprehensive search record.

change_log.change: Explained distinctions across the supplied concept roster while preserving every entry.
change_log.reason: Contact modeling can enable other robotics outcomes without subsuming their separate defining capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any existing model already satisfies the full proposed capability, or whether the selected literature comprehensively represents the field through November 1, 2026.
Billard and Kragic’s attributed structured-abstract statement and the earlier access-history account remain unverified because no retained artifact was supplied.
Zhang’s reported acceptance by npj Robotics is recorded in the research notes but is not independently established by the supplied review.

The proposed task suite, force-and-motion tolerances, prediction horizons, uncertainty coverage, comparability margins, trial counts, safety constraints, and reusable calibration allowances remain to be specified.
The route to the capability—explicit theory, learned prediction, or a hybrid—and the achievable breadth across rigid and deformable interactions remain open.

Cross-entry distinctions beyond ROB-07 rely on roster titles rather than full concept records; the historical common-sense physical reasoning engine description was also not supplied for independent comparison.
